svg.aria-label: Diagram: how the CLASSIC and ENHANCED index modes in Amazon S3 Vectors differ in the order they apply a metadata filter, and what that costs. On the left, the CLASSIC mode, which is what every vector bucket created before 30 September 2026 uses. S3 Vectors performs vector search and filter evaluation in tandem, searching candidate vectors to find the top K most similar while simultaneously validating whether each candidate matches the metadata filter. The consequence, stated in the documentation, is that queries with filters may return fewer than top K results when the index contains very few matching results, so a selective filter leaves a fraction of the real matches and reports no error. On the right, the ENHANCED mode, used by vector buckets created on or after 30 September 2026. Here S3 Vectors first identifies the vectors matching the filter and then searches only those for the most similar ones, which AWS says ensures high recall even when filters match a small fraction of vectors, and which the announcement quantifies as returning up to five times more of the matching vectors when the filter is selective. A central panel records that if pre-filtering returns five times more matches then the old mode could have been surfacing as little as one fifth of them. ENHANCED also unlocks the new dollar startsWith prefix-match operator, which can additionally be used on a CLASSIC index by setting queryMode to ENHANCED on the request, bringing the operator total to twelve alongside equals, not equals, greater than, greater than or equal, less than, less than or equal, in, not in, exists, and, and or. The trade is recorded too: ENHANCED introduces a limit of one hundred filter constraints per query which CLASSIC did not have, where each value evaluated counts as one constraint, and because the filter is evaluated before the search three things increase query latency, namely a larger index, a filter matching a larger share of the vectors, and a filter with more constraints. A closing panel notes that non-filterable metadata keys must be declared at index creation and can never become filterable afterwards, and that exceeding the metadata size limit makes PutVectors return a 400 Bad Request.
svg.title: The filter ran alongside the search, and short results looked like a thin corpus
svg.text: Same filter, same data. The only change is whether it runs before the search.
If pre-filtering returns 5× more matches, the old mode was surfacing as little as a fifth of them.
CLASSIC — buckets created before 30 Sep 2026
search and filter evaluated in tandem:
find top K nearest across the whole index
→ then keep the ones matching the filter
“queries with filters may return fewer than top K
results when the vector index contains very few
matching results”
Ask for 10, get 3, no error. Looks like a thin corpus.
Worst exactly where filters are selective: tenant, permission, date.
ENHANCED — buckets created on or after that date
pre-filtering — filter first, then search:
identify the vectors matching the filter
→ then search only those for nearest
“ensuring high recall even when filters match a
small fraction of vectors”
up to 5× more matching vectors on selective filters
no additional cost · all commercial Regions + China
no change to how you write vectors
Twelve operators now, and the new one makes hierarchical scoping practical
$eq $ne $gt $gte $lt $lte $in $nin $exists $and $or + $startsWith
{"s3_path": {"$startsWith": "/marketing/"}} — and it works on a CLASSIC index too, by setting queryMode to ENHANCED per request.
What ENHANCED costs in exchange
A new limit CLASSIC did not have: 100 filter constraints per query.
Each value counts — so a long $in list adds up.
And latency now depends on the filter: a larger index, a filter matching a larger share, and more constraints all cost more.
So it is fastest where it helps most, and slowest where it helps least. A filter matching 90% is the worst of both.
Audit bucket creation dates. Before 30 September 2026 means CLASSIC, and every filtered query you ran was short.
Compare before migrating: queryMode ENHANCED on a CLASSIC index runs your real queries both ways.
Review any fallback that widens or drops a filter — those were written to compensate for a behaviour that is changing.
Non-filterable metadata keys are declared at index creation and can never be promoted to filterable.
Ask for 10 chunks, get 3, answer from 3 — this is #61’s failure exactly: missing context is indistinguishable from a weak model.
